newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul considers allowing big firms bank management.
newsitem.headline: Seoul considers allowing big firms bank management.

text.p: A South Korean panel said on Tuesday it plans to recommend that big conglomerates be allowed to participate in bank management for the first time.

The plan was among proposals the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform has prepared to improve the backward financial system. The recommendations, aimed at setting the basis for a longer-term financial reform, would be submitted to President Kim Young-sam next week.
The commission said it proposed that reperesentatives of the nation's top five conglomerates be allowed to sit on banks' boards as non-permanent directors.
South Korea currently bans the five business groups, or chaebol, from banking business on fears of growing economic concentration by industrial companies.
But analysts said chaebol's managerial skills would help improve competitiveness of the banking industry.
The commission also said it proposed to lower business barriers between banks, securities houses and insurers.
"They should keep their key business. But it would be better if banks are permitted to issue bonds and if securities houses (are) to engage in foreign exchange business," said a commission official.
The official said the commission would draft another package of proposals by the end of this year on mergers and acquisitions (M&As) in the financial industry and freer bank ownership.
M&As and expanded bank ownership are believed to be necessary to foster large and competitive financial institutions at a time of market liberalisation, analysts said.

Kim said in January the heavily-controlled financial sector urgently needed reform to bring it in line with global trends. He then said a special task force would be set up to draft proposals aimed at streamlining the financial industry.
